slides.title: Solids, liquids and gases
slides.slide: L1 Basic · Solids, liquids and gases
slides.notes: Name the three states of matter and say what happens when a substance is heated. Notes: warm ice in a beaker of warm tap water and record the temperature each minute. Use no flame, and handle warm water with care. Learners say which change is melting.

slides.title: Atoms, elements and compounds
slides.slide: L2 Awareness · Atoms, elements and compounds
slides.notes: Describe atoms, elements and compounds and read simple chemical formulae. Notes: for water, H2O, learners count 2 hydrogen and 1 oxygen, which is 3 atoms in one molecule. They sort symbols into elements and compounds on cards. Wear goggles whenever any chemical is out, even for show-and-tell.

slides.title: Balanced equations and the mole
slides.slide: L3 Foundation · Balanced equations and the mole
slides.notes: Calculate relative formula mass and balance simple equations. Notes: balance 2H2 + O2 gives 2H2O by counting atoms on both sides. Water has Mr 18, so 36 g is 2 mol. Learners repeat this for carbon dioxide, Mr 44, and check that 88 g is 2 mol.

slides.title: Acid-base titration
slides.notes: Apply stoichiometry to find an unknown concentration from a titration. Notes: 25.0 cm3 of sodium hydroxide needs a mean 20.0 cm3 of 0.100 mol/dm3 hydrochloric acid. Moles of acid are 0.00200, equal to moles of alkali, so the alkali is 0.0800 mol/dm3. Wear goggles; use dilute solutions and rinse spills at once.

slides.title: Energy changes and rates
slides.slide: L5 Specialist · Energy changes and rates
slides.notes: Analyse a calorimetry result and link energy change to bond breaking and making. Notes: 50 g of water warms by 6.5 K, so q equals 50 times 4.18 times 6.5, which is 1358.5 J. For 0.025 mol that gives about 54.3 kJ/mol released. Learners list heat loss as the main error and suggest a lid.

slides.title: Thermodynamics and kinetics
slides.notes: Apply Gibbs energy and rate laws to predict whether and how fast a reaction goes. Notes: with change in H of +40 kJ/mol and change in S of +110 J/K/mol at 298 K, G is +7.22 kJ/mol, not spontaneous. It becomes spontaneous above 40000/110, about 364 K. Learners explain why a positive G says nothing about speed.

slides.title: Method validation in analysis
slides.slide: L7 Super expert · Method validation in analysis
slides.notes: Evaluate an analytical method for accuracy, precision and detection limit, and design a validation plan. Notes: with blank noise of 0.002 absorbance and a calibration slope of 0.250 per mg/L, the limit of detection is 3.3 times 0.002 over 0.250, which is 0.0264 mg/L. Write a hazard assessment and waste plan before any lab work.
